newsitem.title: GERMANY: German opposition SPD head backs EMU strongly.
newsitem.headline: German opposition SPD head backs EMU strongly.

text.p: The leader of Germany's opposition Social Democrats (SPD) on Tuesday gave his strongest backing yet to European monetary union, days after his biggest potential party rival called on the SPD to reserve judgment on the issue.
"We want Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) in order to promote growth, employment and stability in all member states," SPD chairman Oskar Lafontaine wrote in the business daily Handelsblatt.

His comments seemed to signal that under his leadership, the SPD would not challenge Chancellor Helmut Kohl's determination to see a single currency introduced on January 1, 1999, nor make it an issue in the run-up to a general election in October 1998.
Any delay would set back the process of convergence among European economies, he wrote, adding:
"To scrap the timetable laid down in the treaty would have far-reaching political consequences -- it would plunge the entire European Union into crisis."

The comments were a rebuff to Lower Saxony premier Gerhard Schroeder, who told Monday's news weekly Focus that the SPD should withhold approval of EMU until it saw what the terms of currency union were and, if necessary, reject them.

Schroeder appealed to the nationalist sentiment courted by some right-wing groups, saying the mark currency was "for west Germans the symbol of their rebirth out of the ruins of fascism and for east Germans a symbol of some kind of chance of a good standard of living and freedom".

Opinion polls regularly indicate well over half the German population oppose or fear the loss of their strong currency and the issue could yet play a role in a general election due in October 1998, just before EMU is supposed to start.
Surveys also suggest the ambitious Schroeder would be the SPD leader most likely to give Kohl a run for his money.

The SPD for its part has not yet decided whether Lafontaine, Schroeder or someone else will spearhead its challenge -- but Schroeder also told Focus he was determined to ensure that EMU was not kept out of the campaign.

Despite Schroeder's popularity in the country at large, he has not so far received overt support from within the SPD for a more Euro-sceptical line and Lafontaine's comments appeared to nail the party's colours strongly to EMU.

He couched his defence of EMU firmly within traditional SPD pro-labour lines, saying it was part of a necessary response to the globalisation and increased competition from abroad which have put German jobs under threat.

"Anyone who thinks Germany can win an economic devaluation race to see which country can pay the lowest real wages, have the lowest corporation taxes and the lowest welfare and environmental standards has failed to understand the global marketplace," he wrote.
"The answer to a more international economy cannot be to renationalise our policies but more international cooperation.

"For us Germans that means above all: We need EMU, as a concerted policy by members aimed at a jointly high standard of living, appropriate and steady growth, high employment, balanced trade and a stable currency."
